title: How to Book KTX Tickets from Seoul to Busan (2026): Korail+ App, Klook, and Prices
html:
If you're planning the classic Seoul–Busan leg of your trip, 2026 is actually a great year to book a KTX (Korea's bullet train) ticket — prices just went down, seats just went up, and the booking rules just got friendlier for foreign travelers. The catch is that almost everything about how you book changed recently, so an old blog post (even from last year) may send you to an app or website that no longer exists in that form. Here's what's actually true right now.

What changed in 2026: KTX and SRT became one system

Until recently, Korea had two separate high-speed train operators that confused a lot of first-timers: KTX (run by Korail, departing mainly from Seoul Station) and SRT (a newer, separate company, departing from Suseo Station in southeast Seoul). On September 1, 2026, the two companies officially merged back into one, and all high-speed trains now run under the single KTX brand (former SRT trains are sometimes labeled KTX-Sancheon). As part of the merger, fares dropped by about 10% and thousands of extra seats were added on weekdays and weekends. This is good news for you: it means lower prices and better availability than what older guides describe.


A KTX high-speed train at Guro Station, Seoul. Since the 2026 Korail–SRT merger, all high-speed trains on this route run under the KTX brand. Photo: Takeshi Aida, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Booking your ticket: the Korail+ app, website, or Klook

You have two solid ways to book, and you don't need to speak Korean for either one:

  • Korail+ app or website (official): This is the renamed version of the old "Korail Talk" app — it merged with the former SRT app in August 2026 so there's now just one official booking app for every high-speed train. On the English version of the site/app, you can book with just an email address, a password, your passport info, and an overseas Visa, Mastercard, or UnionPay card — you do not need a Korean resident ID number. It's the cheapest option since there's no booking fee on top of the ticket price.
  • Klook: Since 2026, Klook isn't just a random third-party reseller — it's an official partner of Korail and Korea's tourism authorities, plugged directly into the real-time KTX reservation system. If the Korail+ app feels confusing or glitchy on your phone (a common complaint from first-time foreign users), Klook's app is a friendlier backup with a more familiar, English-first interface.

Be more cautious with other, unaffiliated third-party booking sites or apps that charge a markup "service fee" to book a KTX seat for you — some are fine, but since they're not officially connected to Korail, it's hard to guarantee refunds or support if something goes wrong. When in doubt, the official Korail+ app/website or Klook are the two options worth trusting.

Prices, booking windows, and the Korail Pass question

Here's what to actually expect at checkout:

  • Price: A one-way adult standard-class seat from Seoul Station to Busan Station currently runs about 54,400 KRW (down from 59,800 KRW before the 2026 fare cut). A non-reserved seat is a little cheaper, and first class runs noticeably more.
  • Journey time: Around 2 hours 10 minutes to 2 hours 45 minutes, depending on how many stops your train makes along the way.
  • How far ahead you can book: As of October 1, 2026, Korail doubled the booking window from 30 days to 60 days before departure — a change made specifically because so many foreign tourists were trying to book further ahead than the old window allowed. Take advantage of it, especially for weekend travel or anything around Chuseok (Korean Thanksgiving) or Lunar New Year, when seats sell out fast.
  • Korail Pass: You'll see this unlimited-ride foreigner pass advertised everywhere (roughly 131,000 KRW and up for the shortest 2-day version). For a single one-way Seoul–Busan trip, skip it — the cheapest pass already costs more than double your actual ticket. It only starts to make sense if you're taking several long-distance train trips within a few days.

Seat reservations, and why the station name on your ticket still matters

You don't strictly need a reserved seat — non-reserved or standing tickets are usually available even when reserved seats sell out, bought at a station kiosk or ticket counter. That said, book a reserved seat ahead of time if you can, especially around holidays, since "non-reserved" can mean standing for over two hours during Chuseok or Seollal.

One more thing worth double-checking: even though booking is now unified under one app, your train may still depart from either Seoul Station (central Seoul) or Suseo Station (southeast Seoul, near Gangnam) — the old KTX/SRT station split didn't fully disappear just because the companies merged. Always check the departure station printed on your ticket or app screen, not just the time. Both stations connect directly to the Seoul subway, so you won't need a taxi to reach either one.


Both Seoul Station and Suseo Station connect directly to the Seoul subway system. Photo: LWY, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

How Koreans actually book their tickets

Most Korean travelers just open the Korail+ app directly, the same way you'd open any transit app — they rarely bother with third-party apps at all, since the official app is already in Korean and linked to their usual payment methods. The one thing locals do that's worth copying: they set a phone reminder for the moment a popular departure (like a Friday evening train before a holiday) opens for booking, because the best times still disappear within minutes once a long weekend is announced.

Quick comparison: where should you book?

Where to book Booking fee English support Best for
Korail+ app/website (official) None — pay list price Yes, English booking flow Cheapest option, confident solo bookers
Klook (official Korail partner) None confirmed for KTX booking Yes, very foreigner-friendly First-timers who want a familiar app
Other third-party resellers Often a markup fee Varies Not recommended unless official options fail
Korail Pass Flat pass price (131,000 KRW+) Yes Multiple long-distance trips only, not a single one-way ride
